Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

This artist's illustration indicates the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

It has been revealed that dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

It has been revealed that dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â stated Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

Recent findings suggest that this image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and indicates the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

According to recent reports, euclid introduced in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Big Bang.

In a recent development, among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 upcoming strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

Recent findings suggest that "Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â said Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 latest candidates.â.

There's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row highlights, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

Sources indicate that overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â remarked Srivastava.

Sources indicate that strong gravitational lensing is an vital tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

In a recent development, finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly important in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Substantial Bang model of cosmology.

Sources indicate that lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one big grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each newly introduced data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

Recent findings suggest that but that won't be the end of cosmology. Upcoming questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

According to recent reports, in other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a latest study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

According to recent reports, at Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

It has been revealed that the gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its massive flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

Industry observers note that I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

According to recent reports, it's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll rapidly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

In a recent development, as a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An experimental drug helped mice resist cancers their immune systems had never encountered, raising the possibility that treating one tumor could someday help protect against others.
  • Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most difficult cancers to treat, partly because tumors can wall themselves off from the immune system.
  • Industry observers note that researchers have now developed an experimental drug that breaks through this barrier in mice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experimental drug helped mice resist cancers their immune systems had never encountered, raising the possibility that treating one tumor could someday help protect against others.

Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most difficult cancers to treat, partly because tumors can wall themselves off from the immune system. Many breast, colon, and lung cancers use the same defense, surrounding themselves with dense, scar-like tissue that keeps cancer-fighting immune cells out. This barrier is one reason immunotherapy, which helps the immune system attack cancer, works for only a minority of patients with solid tumors.

Industry observers note that researchers have now developed an experimental drug that breaks through this barrier in mice. The treatment eliminated aggressive pancreatic tumors in some animals, prevented breast cancer from spreading, and produced lasting immune protection against future cancers.

The study, published November 9, 2026, in Cancer Cell, was led by Seong-Jin Kim, PhD, and scientists at MedPacto, Inc., in Seoul, Korea.

Sources indicate that tumors build their defenses partly by releasing large amounts of a chemical messenger called TGF-β. This substance encourages nearby cells to produce fibrous tissue while weakening the immune cells that could attack the cancer. Blocking it has proven difficult because TGF-β also performs important functions in healthy tissue. Previous drugs have struggled to suppress enough of it inside tumors without causing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

To get around this problem, the team developed a drug called FEBP-sTβRII that carries a molecular tag directing it toward tumors. The tag attaches to a particular form of fibronectin, a protein abundant in many cancers but rarely found in healthy adult tissue. Researchers detected this target in mouse models of breast, colon, lung, liver, prostate, pancreatic, and brain cancers, as well as melanoma, and in many human tumor types.

According to recent reports, the targeted drug accumulated inside tumors and remained there for days. Without the tag, the same blocker had little effect on tumors and altered the activity of 693 genes in the blood, compared with just 25 for the targeted treatment.

“This study reveals that where you block TGF-β matters as much as whether you block it,” said senior author Kim, who is also affiliated with the GILO Institute.

Sources indicate that with the protective barrier weakened, cancer-killing T cells could enter the tumors. They released a chemical signal called interferon-gamma, prompting nearby support cells and immune cells to display recognizable pieces of the cancer. This helped the immune system identify its target and sustain the attack. Researchers observed this response in pancreatic tumors and melanoma.

Unlike existing immunotherapies that primarily remove restrictions on T cells, the experimental drug also changes the environment surrounding the cancer, making it easier for immune cells to reach and recognize tumors.

The researchers reported several promising results across different mouse experiments:.

“TGF-β helps build the defenses of many solid tumors, so this approach has the potential to reach well beyond a single cancer,” said Dr. Letterio. “By delivering the blocker directly to the tumor, we don’t just open the door to T cells. We appear to be teaching the immune system lessons it remembers long after the tumor is gone, and in some cases those lessons protect against other cancers.”.

In a recent development, study co-author John J. Letterio, MD, PhD, directs the Angie Fowler Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Institute at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies & Children’s Hospital and the Developmental Therapeutics Program at Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, Case Western Reserve University.

The immune response observed in mice resembled patterns previously seen in patients who responded to immunotherapy for melanoma, gastric cancer, and pancreatic cancer. Measuring the drug’s fibronectin target in tumors might eventually help identify patients most likely to benefit.

A human version of the drug has entered safety testing, with clinical trials planned for 2027 to evaluate its safety and effectiveness in patients whose solid tumors have not responded to standard treatments.

In a recent development, reference: “A stroma-sensing TGF-β blockade reprograms CAF-myeloid niches to induce durable tumor immunity” by Dong Woo Kang, Jin Beom Bae, Seonho Yoo, Hyejin Kim, Pyunggang Kim, Jaewoo Mo, Jinhwan Kim, Jin Su Kim, Kwiyeom Yoon, Ye Seon Kim, Jeong Su Lee, June Myoung Kim, Min Gi Kang, Min Jung Lee, Changwon Lim, Isaac Y. Kim, Chang Pyo Hong, Junil Kim, John J. Letterio and Seong-Jin Kim, 09 November 2026, Cancer Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.ccell.2026.10.007.

Disclosure: Dr. Kim is a founder of MedPacto and co-founder of Celloram. Dr. Letterio is a co-founder of Celloram and a member of MedPacto’s clinical advisory board. MedPacto holds pending patents on the drug.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

It has been revealed that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

Sources indicate that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

According to recent reports, in the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

But why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

In a recent development, but ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1203 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why Sleeping 9 Hours After 50 May Be a Warning Sign for Your Career

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.
  • Recent findings suggest that as retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older.
  • People with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.

Recent findings suggest that as retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older. A large Finnish study suggests that sleep may be part of the picture. Adults who frequently struggled with sleep after age 50 tended to spend fewer years working, while those who regularly slept nine hours or more a night also had shorter expected working lives.

People with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems. Among people who slept at least nine hours a night, the gap ranged from roughly nine months to more than two years, depending on the study group.

The findings, published online in Occupational & Environmental Medicine, come as more than half of the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have raised statutory retirement ages in response to aging populations. Previous research has explored why people leave their jobs early, including disability, illness, and retirement decisions. However, researchers had not examined whether sleep duration and quality were associated with how long people remain employed.

To investigate, the team focused on working life expectancy, which measures the average number of years someone can expect to remain employed at a particular age. Rather than measuring how long people live, the researchers examined their expected years in the workforce between ages 50 and 68.

The analysis drew on two Finnish studies involving more than 76,000 adults. The Finnish Public Sector (FPS) study included 70,339 public sector employees between 2000 and 2016, approximately 80% of whom were women. The Health and Social Support (HeSSup) study provided a random sample of 6,071 working-age Finnish adults between 1998 and 2013, with women accounting for 54% of participants. Researchers assessed sleep using the first survey each participant completed after turning 50, then examined employment information from the Earnings and Accrual Register, maintained by the Finnish Centre for Pensions.

The surveys asked participants how long they usually slept and how often they experienced difficulties falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, or feeling unrested after sleeping. These disturbances were assessed over the preceding four weeks. People who experienced them no more than once a week were considered to have no sleep disturbances, while those reporting problems two to four nights a week were placed in the moderate category. Severe disturbances meant experiencing these problems five or six nights a week to nearly every night. Sleep duration was classified separately as short, meaning less than seven hours, mid-range at seven to eight and a half hours, or long at nine hours or more.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a consistent relationship between disrupted sleep and fewer expected years of employment. Participants without sleep disturbances had an average working life expectancy of 13 years and five months after age 50. That fell to approximately 13 years among those with moderate disturbances and 12 years and 10 months among those with severe problems. Compared with people reporting no disturbances, these groups could expect to work nearly five and eight fewer months, respectively. The association appeared among both men and women and across three broad occupational categories: professional, intermediate, and routine jobs.

Sources indicate that employment differences became more apparent when researchers examined sleep alongside occupation and sex. Professional women who reported no sleep disturbances had the longest expected working lives in this comparison, at nearly 14 years after age 50. Men in routine jobs who experienced severe sleep disturbances had the shortest, at approximately 12 and a half years.

Sleep duration revealed a somewhat different pattern. In the Finnish Public Sector study, participants sleeping fewer than seven hours a night and those sleeping between seven and eight and a half hours had the same average working life expectancy of 13 years and two months. Those who regularly slept nine hours or more, however, had an expected working life of just 12 years and five months. Compared with the mid-range sleep group, that represented approximately nine fewer months of employment.

The association was even stronger in the HeSSup study, where sleeping nine hours or more was linked to just over 30 fewer months of expected employment compared with sleeping seven to eight and a half hours. Researchers found no clear evidence that people sleeping fewer than seven hours had shorter working lives than those in the mid-range category, regardless of sex or job type.

It has been revealed that education and occupation also appeared to shape these patterns. When researchers compared the most advantaged participants, those with professional jobs or higher education and no sleep disturbances or short to mid-range sleep, with the least advantaged, those in routine jobs or with lower education and severe sleep problems or long sleep, the differences were considerable. The gap in expected working life was approximately one year and five months in the FPS group and five years in the HeSSup group.

Recent findings suggest that in a more detailed analysis combining sleep duration with socioeconomic circumstances, 50-year-old men and women in professional jobs who reported short nightly sleep had the longest expected working lives in the FPS study, at around 13 years and seven months. In HeSSup, highly educated women had the longest working life expectancy, at approximately 11 and a half years. At the other extreme, men in routine jobs or with lower levels of education who regularly slept nine hours or more had an expected working life of only about six years and five months in both study groups.

Although the findings suggest a connection between sleep and working life, they do not establish that poor sleep or longer sleep directly causes people to leave employment earlier. The study was observational, and the researchers could not account for several potentially influential factors, including physical and mental health, underlying medical conditions, risky health behaviors, and working conditions such as shift work. These factors could affect both sleep patterns and the ability to remain employed.

Still, the findings suggest that helping people manage sleep problems in midlife may be worth considering as countries look for ways to support longer working careers, particularly among people facing socioeconomic disadvantages.

“Promoting sleep health and providing support for managing sleep disturbances at midlife may be especially notable for those with a lower socioeconomic status when aiming to increase workforce participation with advancing age,” the researchers concluded.

“This could include cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia delivered by occupational health services or workplace interventions, such as educational or health promotion interventions for sleep.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Sleep disturbances and sleep duration as predictors of working life expectancy among adults aged 50 years and older in Finland” by Saana Myllyntausta, Katriina Heikkilä, Jaana Pentti, Holendro Singh Chungkham, Sakari Suominen, Mika Kivimaki, Jussi Vahtera, Paola Zaninotto, Jenni Ervasti and Sari Stenholm, 18 August 2026, Occupational and Environmental Medicine. DOI: 10.1136/oemed-2025-110766.

Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system.
  • Recent findings suggest that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a substantial part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one major system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a newly introduced trick with them: photosynthesis.

Recent findings suggest that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

But this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

Newly introduced research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

Recent findings suggest that the oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

In a recent development, the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on fresh geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide fresh constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

They found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

In a recent development, the researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

This graphic illustrates the results from newly introduced research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that shows how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Recent findings suggest that on shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it demonstrates that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

It has been revealed that over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

Recent findings suggest that "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

This figure demonstrates the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

According to recent reports, it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work highlights that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

Industry observers note that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
  • On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

Recent findings suggest that “Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.).

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

In a recent development, scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” states planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

According to recent reports, “Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” claims planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always revealed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” indicates planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

It has been revealed that similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

Breaking: Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • According to recent reports, earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Recent findings suggest that understanding why this is crucial requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a fresh paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

According to recent reports, earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Recent findings suggest that understanding why this is crucial requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

Industry observers note that what was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study highlighted that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

Recent findings suggest that with that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

Combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.

#19794. New FDA-Approved Pill Lowers High Blood Pressure and May Slow Kidney Disease

New FDA-Approved Pill Lowers High Blood Pressure and May Slow Kidney Disease

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.
  • A drug that showed early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication.
  • The approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.

A drug that showed early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication. Called Baxfendy (baxdrostat), the treatment targets a hormone involved in both hypertension and kidney disease.

The approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions. Earlier research also found that baxdrostat lowered a key marker of kidney damage by 55%, suggesting potential benefits beyond hypertension. Whether the medication can slow kidney disease progression remains under investigation.

According to recent reports, the FDA approved AstraZeneca’s Baxfendy in May 2026 for adults whose hypertension remains inadequately controlled by existing treatments. It is the first approved aldosterone synthase inhibitor, a class of drugs that reduces production of the hormone aldosterone.

It has been revealed that in the Phase 3 BaxHTN trial involving 796 patients, the 2 mg dose reduced systolic blood pressure by an average of 15.7 mm Hg after 12 weeks, compared with 5.8 mm Hg for placebo. The additional reduction of 9.8 mm Hg was statistically significant. A lower 1 mg dose also produced meaningful improvements.

In a recent development, dr. Bryan Williams, Chair of Medicine at University College London and the trial’s primary investigator, noted: “We have been waiting for an innovative medication like Baxfendy for hypertension for many years. Its novel way of lowering blood pressure has the potential to transform clinical practice by targeting a root cause of persistently uncontrolled hypertension. In addition, the nearly double-digit placebo-adjusted systolic blood pressure reduction achieved with Baxfendy is exciting and clinically meaningful for clinicians and patients. Epidemiological data indicate that a 10 mmHg decrease in systolic blood pressure is associated with a roughly 20% lower risk of serious cardiovascular events.”.

In a recent development, aldosterone regulates sodium and water balance in the body. Excessive levels cause the kidneys to retain fluid, increasing blood pressure and potentially contributing to kidney inflammation and scarring.

Baxdrostat inhibits the enzyme responsible for producing aldosterone rather than blocking the hormone’s receptors, as some existing medications do. This approach may benefit patients whose blood pressure remains high despite multiple treatments.

A separate Phase 3 trial, Bax24, involving 218 patients found that baxdrostat lowered average systolic blood pressure over 24 hours by 14.0 mm Hg more than placebo. The effect persisted throughout the day and night, according to findings published in The Lancet.

High blood pressure and chronic kidney disease can worsen each other. Elevated pressure damages the kidneys’ filtering structures, while declining kidney function makes hypertension harder to control.

“These findings are encouraging for people living with chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure, two conditions that often go hand-in-hand and create a dangerous cycle,” noted lead study author Jamie P. Dwyer, M.D., a professor of medicine at University of Utah Health. “High blood pressure can worsen kidney function and declining kidney function can further elevate blood pressure, and these outcomes can be life-altering for patients.”.

According to recent reports, in the Phase 2 FigHTN trial, 192 patients with chronic kidney disease and uncontrolled hypertension were randomly assigned to receive baxdrostat or placebo alongside standard treatment. After 26 weeks, systolic blood pressure fell an average of 8.1 mm Hg more in the baxdrostat groups.

Researchers also measured urinary albumin, a protein associated with kidney damage when present in elevated amounts. Levels were 55% lower in patients receiving baxdrostat than in those taking placebo. The findings were published in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

The earlier kidney disease trial found elevated blood potassium in 41% of baxdrostat recipients, compared with 5% of placebo recipients. Most cases were mild or moderate, but excessive potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythm disturbances. Serious adverse events occurred in 9% and 3% of participants, respectively.

Although subsequent Phase 3 hypertension studies reported no unexpected safety findings, potassium levels and kidney function require monitoring during treatment.

Recent findings suggest that “The reduction in urine albumin gives us hope that baxdrostat may also help delay kidney damage. This potential is now being tested in two large Phase 3 trials to determine if baxdrostat delays the progression of kidney disease,” stated Dwyer.

Industry observers note that larger studies are investigating whether baxdrostat can preserve kidney function over time, including trials combining it with dapagliflozin, an established kidney-protective medication. Its FDA approval currently covers hypertension, not the prevention of kidney disease progression.

In a recent development, “These new findings are reassuring that this new class of antihypertensive medications are likely to have both kidney- and cardio-protective benefits and to be safe and effective for broad patient populations,” stated Jordana B. Cohen, M.D., M.S.C.E., immediate past chair of the American Heart Association’s Hypertension and Kidney Cardiovascular Science Committee. “Patients with chronic kidney disease were historically often excluded from drug studies. It is particularly reassuring to know that patients with chronic kidney disease, who have very high rates of hypertension and elevated renin-angiotensin aldosterone activity, were represented in their own study, tolerated the medication well, and had both blood pressure and albuminuric benefits. This medication class could be a game changer in the management of hypertension in this patient group.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Efficacy and Safety of Baxdrostat in Participants with CKD and Uncontrolled Hypertension: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial” by Jamie P. Dwyer, Noha Maklad, Ola Vedin, John Monyak, Robin Myte, Glenn M. Chertow, Hiddo J.L. Heerspink and Dustin J. Little, 6 September 2025, Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • Industry observers note that astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Industry observers note that astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

Industry observers note that the common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

It has been revealed that this simple graphic shows how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

In a recent development, this is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

Recent findings suggest that observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in upcoming research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

In a recent development, that much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

According to recent reports, astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

Recent findings suggest that âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â mentioned first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

Sources indicate that stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

According to recent reports, âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â noted co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Latest York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

It has been revealed that this is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel reveals the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

In a recent development, since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an important role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

As in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an crucial role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

It has been revealed that that work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

Industry observers note that the astronomers called the pair Big Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

According to recent reports, these artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

"The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

According to recent reports, "In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory claims that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

But this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

Sources indicate that this work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

Latest Update: Mysterious Radio Signals From 5,000 Light-Years Away Lead Scientists to a Surprising Discovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.
  • Mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours.
  • Now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an notable clue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.

Mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours. Astronomers have found only about a dozen of these unusual sources, and one question has been especially difficult to answer: What is actually producing the pulses?

Now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an notable clue. Known as GPM J071507−114153, it contains a white dwarf, the dense core left behind after a star dies, orbiting a companion remarkably similar to our Sun. The white dwarf spins once every eight minutes.

The discovery is unusual because astronomers have never before detected these radio pulses from a white dwarf paired with a Sun-like star. Previously identified systems producing similar signals have typically involved much smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs.

Sources indicate that these mysterious sources belong to a class called long-period transients (LPTs). Since researchers at the International Center for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) first discovered one in 2021, around a dozen have been identified. Several contain a white dwarf and another star, although astronomers have struggled to determine which one produces the radio signals.

Scientists at the Curtin University node at the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun. Credit: Natasha Hurley-Walker.

In the newly discovered system, scientists finally had enough information to narrow down the source.

“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” noted Dr Sam McSweeney, the study’s lead author and a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory.

McSweeney made the discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. To confirm and better understand the white dwarf’s movement, the team processed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Center.

Industry observers note that the radio pulses also revealed something unexpected about the white dwarf’s companion. Researchers detected evidence of stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to the activity associated with auroras here on Earth.

“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”.

The observation suggests astronomers can use radio signals to investigate magnetic activity on distant stars, even when those stars are thousands of light-years away.

“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”.

Both observations were described by Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, a co-author of the paper.

Finding such a rare system required several powerful telescopes working together. The researchers first identified its radio signals during a large survey of the Milky Way, then used additional observations to pinpoint its location.

It has been revealed that “We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

It has been revealed that once the radio source had been located, optical observations from the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star, the same broad class as our Sun.

It has been revealed that the MWA, led by Curtin University, is located at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia. MeerKAT, meanwhile, was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa’s North Cape province.

Both facilities are precursors to the larger SKA telescopes now being developed, SKA-Low in Australia and SKA-Mid in South Africa. These future observatories are expected to provide more detailed observations of unusual radio sources and help astronomers identify additional systems that have so far escaped detection.

“If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built,” stated Dr McSweeney.

Sources indicate that reference: “A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion” by Samuel J. McSweeney, Natasha Hurley-Walker, Arash Bahramian, Csanád Horváth, Nanda Rea, Antonio C. Rodriguez and Ingrid Pelisoli, 12 November 2026, Nature Astronomy. DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-03016-z.
